title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based lessons for training novice human tutors in middle school mathematics. The authors focus on a practical curriculum-design problem: creating structured tutor training lessons is time-consuming and hard to scale, so they investigate whether an LLM can produce lessons that are pedagogically sound, clear, and useful for instructional design.

The intervention is not a student-facing tutoring treatment but a lesson-generation pipeline built with retrieval-augmented generation and GPT-4o. The system generates English-language tutor training lessons around three middle-school math tutoring topics: encouraging students’ independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras. The authors compare several prompting strategies that vary in task decomposition, from generating a whole lesson in one step to splitting it into five segments.

The study evaluates the generated lessons with two experienced human coders using a rubric, and also collects written feedback from two expert lesson designers who compared LLM-generated lessons with human-crafted ones. The context is an online tutor-training platform for novice tutors teaching middle school mathematics. The main finding is that moderate task decomposition worked best: the three-segment approach produced the highest-rated lessons, while one-step generation was weakest and five segments was not better than three. The generated lessons were seen as useful for saving time and producing realistic scenarios, but they also had important weaknesses, especially generic feedback, unclear or overly verbose instructions, and unreliable references. The paper concludes that LLMs can support lesson design as part of a human-AI workflow, but human review remains necessary.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative human-evaluation study of LLM-generated lesson content with coder agreement (Cohen’s κ=0.72), but it is not an experimental study of learner outcomes and does not include a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison on student achievement. It provides useful evidence about content quality and workflow, but with limited causal credibility for educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest positive effects on lesson quality and clear time-saving potential, but it does not measure any direct impact on student learning, so educational impact remains unclear. The main demonstrated gains are operational rather than achievement-related.

interventions.use_case: Retrieval-augmented GPT-4o lesson-generation system for creating scenario-based tutor training lessons for novice human tutors teaching middle school mathematics online; compared one- to five-segment prompt decomposition strategies and human-crafted lesson designs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM-assisted lesson generation substantially saves time in drafting tutor-training materials, especially for scenario sections and multiple-choice questions. Two lesson designers reported that GPT-generated lessons reduce repetitive drafting and research burden, with the three-segment approach receiving the highest average quality rating (14.67/17) while being considered efficient for iterative refinement; however, no learning-outcome effect sizes were reported because student achievement was not measured.
finding.measure: Human expert ratings of lesson quality plus qualitative designer feedback on time savings and drafting workload
finding.study_size: n=3 generated lessons per prompting condition, rated by 2 human coders; 2 lesson designers interviewed for comparison

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that LLMs can support scalable production of tutor-training content for online middle school mathematics programs, potentially expanding access to professional development. The best-performing decomposition strategy was three segments, which improved overall lesson ratings versus one segment (14.67 vs 10.67 average rubric score), but the paper did not evaluate downstream student outcomes or institutional adoption at scale.
finding.measure: Expert rubric ratings of generated lessons and qualitative assessment of scalability/value for tutor training programs
finding.study_size: n=3 lesson topics across 5 prompting strategies; 2 expert coders; 2 lesson designers for comparison
